To impose (on) for one's advantage; to be presumptuous; to take advantage (of); to take liberties (with) [with on or upon].
d.x: Thanks, but I can't accept the money; I would not want to presume on the generosity of a stranger'

presume.e: From Middle English presumen, from Anglo-Norman presumer and its source, Latin praesūmere (“to take beforehand, anticipate”), from prae- + sūmere (“to take”).

d.g: To assume some truth without proof, usually for the purpose of reaching a conclusion based on that truth.

presuppose.e: From Middle French presupposer, from Latin praesuppōnō.

d.g: To intentionally disregard (something), to ignore; to neglect or omit.
d.x: [F]or the public, for the redemption of the whole world, God hath (shall we say, pretermitted?) derelicted, forsaken, abandoned, his own, and only Son.

d.g: To make pretty or prettier, to make more attractive, especially only in a superficial way.
d.x: Old-fashioned bosses see their role as prettifying the office and forming a pool of potential marriage partners for male employees.

d.g: Synonym of pretty-print.

prettify.e: English pretty English -fy English prettify From pretty + -fy.

d.g: To be superior in strength, dominance, influence, or frequency; to have or gain the advantage over others; to have the upper hand; to outnumber others.

d.g: To triumph; to be victorious.
To be current, widespread, or predominant; to have currency or prevalence.
d.x: In his day and age, such practices prevailed all over Europe.

d.g: To succeed in persuading or inducing.
d.x: I prevailed on him to wait.

prevail.e: From Middle English prevailen, from Old French prevaler, from Latin praevaleō (“be very able or more able, be superior, prevail”), from prae (“before”) + valeō (“be able or powerful”). Displaced native Old English rīcsian.

d.g: To speak or act in a manner that is intentionally ambiguous or evasive; equivocate.
d.x: The people saw the politician prevaricate every day.

d.g: To collude, as where an informer colludes with the defendant, and makes a sham prosecution.
To undertake something falsely and deceitfully, with the purpose of defeating or destroying it.

prevaricate.e: Borrowed from Latin praevāricātus, perfect active participle of praevāricor (“to walk crookedly; to play a false or double part”), from prae- + vāricō (“to stand with feet apart, straddle”), from vāricus (“with feet spread apart”); see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

d.g: To stop (an outcome); to keep from (doing something).
d.x: I brush my teeth regularly to prevent tooth decay.

prevent.e: From Middle English preventen (“anticipate”), from Latin praeventus, perfect passive participle of praeveniō (“to anticipate”), from prae (“before”) + veniō (“to come”).

d.g: To foresee.
d.x: try to divine the inevitable fortunes of your friends, and of the leaders and rulers of nations; endeavour to previse and forewarn; and study proleptics.

d.g: To forewarn.

previse.e: From Latin praevisus, the past participle of praevideō.

d.g: To spend time improving one's appearance, often in front of a mirror.
d.x: "Then I promise I'll let you take your bath and primp all day for your date."

d.g: To dress in an affected manner.
The act of adjusting one's dress or appearance; the act of sprucing oneself up.
d.x: “Is my sash right; and does my hair look very bad?” said Meg, as she turned from the glass in Mrs. Gardiner’s dressing-room, after a prolonged prink.

d.g: To look, gaze.
To dress finely, primp, preen, spruce up.
d.x: […] by the Mass: You’ll make excellent Wives, Cuckold your Husbands immoderately: You mind nothing but prinking your selves up.

d.g: To strut, put on pompous airs, be pretentious.

prink.e: From Middle English prinken (“to wink, signal with the eye”), from prinke, prinche (“a wink, twinkling of the eye, momentary gesture”), from Old English princ (“a wink”). More at pry.

d.g: UK standard spelling of prioritize.

prioritise.e: English priority English -ise English prioritise From priority + -ise.

d.g: To value, do, or choose something first, or before other things.
d.x: When I don't have time to buy everything at the store, I prioritize fresh fruit and vegetables over foods like rice or noodles.

d.g: To arrange or list a group of things in order of priority or importance.
To rank something as having high priority.

prioritize.e: From priority + -ize. First attested in 1967 as U.S. government jargon, becoming more widespread through the 1970s and ’80s, but still denounced as officialese by purists into the 1990s.

d.g: To force (open) with a lever; to pry.
d.x: I think he must have been trying to prise open that box yonder when he was attacked.

d.g: To extract something that is difficult to obtain.

prise.e: From the Middle English noun prise (“taking of something”), from Old French prise (“seizure; taking; capture”), past participle of prendre (“to take”). Doublet of prize.

d.g: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of privatize.

privatise.e: English private English -ise English privatise From private + -ise.

d.g: To release government control (of a business or industry) to private industry.
To render (a variable, etc.) private in scope.

d.g: To render a thought or an idea, private in scope.
d.x: The neoliberal, privatizing version of health in which everyone is responsible for themselves, despite disparities in resources.

d.g: To go on in an orderly or regulated manner; to begin and carry on a series of acts or measures; to act methodically.

proceed.e: From Middle English proceden, from Old French proceder, from Latin prōcēdō (“to go forth, go forward, advance”), from prō (“forth”) + cēdō (“to go”); see cede.

d.g: To announce or declare.
To make (something) the subject of an official proclamation bringing it within the scope of emergency powers.
d.x: Were those baronies proclaimed at the time you were in them? –Some of them are; the barony of Duhallow is proclaimed.

proclaim.e: From Middle English proclamen, proclaime, from Old French proclamer, from Latin prōclāmō, prōclāmāre, from prō- (“forth”) + clāmō (“to shout, cry out”). Spelling altered by influence of claim, from the same Latin source (clāmō).

d.g: To delay taking action; to wait until later.

d.g: To put off; to delay (something).

procrastinate.e: First attested in 1548; from Latin prōcrastinātus, perfect passive participle of prōcrastinō (“defer, put off till tomorrow”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from prō- (“in favor of”) + crāstinus (“of or belonging to tomorrow”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix), from crās (“tomorrow”).

d.g: To beget or conceive (offsprings).
To originate, create or produce.
To reproduce.

d.g: To acquire or obtain.

d.g: To obtain a person as a prostitute for somebody else.
To induce or persuade someone to do something.

procure.e: From Middle English procuren, from Old French procurer, from Late Latin prōcūrāre (“to manage, administer”), from prō (“on behalf of”) + cūrō (“to care for”).

d.g: To administer the vows of a religious order to (someone); to admit to a religious order.

d.g: To declare oneself (to be something).

d.g: To declare; to assert, affirm.

d.g: To make a claim (to be something); to lay claim to (a given quality, feeling etc.), often with connotations of insincerity.

profess.e: From Old French professer, and its source, the participle stem of Latin profitērī, from pro- + fatērī (“to confess, acknowledge”).

d.g: Alternative spelling of professionalize.

To advance an occupation to the level of a profession.

d.g: To predict or forecast, especially through the application of skill.

d.g: To increase in number or spread rapidly; to multiply.

d.g: Alternative form of prologuize.

d.g: To extend in space or length.

d.g: To become longer; lengthen.

d.g: To advocate or urge on behalf of (something or someone); to attempt to popularize or sell by means of advertising or publicity.

d.g: To put into effect as a regulation.
To advocate on behalf of (something or someone, especially of an idea); to spread knowledge of and make more widely known.

d.g: To turn or rotate one’s hand and forearm so that the palm faces down if the forearm is horizontal, back if the arm is pointing down, or forward if the forearm is pointing up; to twist the right forearm counterclockwise or the left forearm clockwise.
To twist the foot so that if walking the weight would be borne on the inner edge of the foot.
To become pronated.
Somewhat prone; inclined.
d.x: pronate trees

pronate.e: From Latin prōnatus, past participle of prōnare (“to bend forward”). See prone.

d.g: To jump with all four limbs at once.
d.x: Like stotting, pronking is a signal of medium excitation and is performed more often by fawns than by adults (1, 16).

d.g: A gait or a leap in which all four legs are used to push off the ground at once.

pronk.e: From Afrikaans pronk (“to show off, strut, or prance”), from Dutch pronken (“to show off, be flamboyant”). See also prank.

d.g: To declare formally, officially or ceremoniously.

d.g: To pronounce dead.

d.g: To pass judgment.

d.g: To check a written text for errors in spelling, grammar, syntax, and punctuation.

d.g: Alternative form of propagandize.

d.g: To use something or someone in propaganda purposes.

To cause to spread to extend; to impel or continue forward in space.

To generate; to produce.

propagate.e: First attested in 1535; from Latin prōpāgātus, perfect passive participle of prōpāgō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Participial usage up until Early Modern English.

d.g: To provide an impetus for motion or physical action; to cause to move in a certain direction; to drive or push forward.

propel.e: From Middle English propellen (“drive out, expel”), from Latin propellō, from pro- (“forward”) and pellō (“to push, to move”).

No, but when the Spirit fils

Then I perceive that will be verified
Henry the Fifth did sometime prophesy
‘If once he come to be a cardinal,
He’ll make his cap co-equal with the crown.’

d.g: To foreshow; to herald; to prefigure.

d.g: To speak out on the Bible as an expression of holy inspiration; to preach.

prophesy.e: From Middle English prophecien; partly from prophecie, and partly from Middle French prophecier, prophesier, from prophecie (“prophecy”). Doublet of prophecy.

d.g: To conciliate, appease, or make peace with someone, particularly a god or spirit.

d.g: To make propitious or favourable.
To make propitiation.

d.g: To suggest a plan, course of action, etc.

d.g: To ask for a person's hand in marriage.

d.g: To intend.

d.g: To put forward; to offer for discussion or debate.

d.g: To divide proportionately, especially by day; to divide pro rata.

d.g: To suspend (a parliamentary session) or to discontinue the meetings of (an assembly, parliament etc.) without formally ending the session.

prorogue.e: From Old French proroger, proroguer, from Latin prōrogō (“prolong, defer”).

d.g: command against
